content: Polymorphous light eruption (PLE), also known as polymorphic light eruption, is a dermatological condition triggered by exposure to sunlight. The condition manifests as skin irritations, which can be either itchy or painful, and are sometimes mistaken for hives. These skin reactions typically occur after sun exposure, with as little as 15 minutes of sunlight being sufficient to provoke symptoms. The duration of these symptoms can range from 1 to 7 days. In most cases, PLE resolves spontaneously without the need for medical intervention, and the skin lesions generally heal without leaving scars. The condition is most frequently observed during the spring and summer months in the northern hemisphere. Epidemiological data suggest that PLE affects approximately 10-20% of the population, with a higher prevalence in females compared to males. It can occur across all ethnic groups, and studies indicate that around 20% of affected individuals have a family history of the condition. PLE typically presents before the age of 30. The exact etiology of PLE remains unclear, but it is hypothesized to involve a type IV delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction. In terms of diagnosis, physical examination of the skin is essential. Visual documentation of PLE lesions is often referenced from dermatological atlases to aid in clinical identification. As of 2008, experimental treatments for PLE have been under investigation. An Australian company, Clinuvel Pharmaceuticals Limited, has been conducting clinical trials using a melanocyte-stimulating hormone called melanotan (referred to as CUV1647) as a potential therapeutic option for managing PLE.
